forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: South Oxfordshire's investments earned £8.6m in 2025/26, above budget; Vale's earned £6.4m
news_drafts.lead:
South Oxfordshire District Council's treasury investments earned £8.6 million in 2025/26, more than the council had budgeted. The figure is in the treasury management outturn report for the year. Treasury management is how a council invests its spare cash and manages its borrowing, and outturn means the actual figures once the year has ended. The report goes to the full Council on 22 October.

The same report gives £6.4 million for the neighbouring Vale of White Horse District Council, which also exceeded its budget. The report says both councils beat their budgeted investment income, but the material does not give South's budget figure.

Vale's own treasury appendix, in a cabinet paper dated 8 October 2026, sets out its result in more detail. It earned £6,401,000 against a budget of £4,342,000, a difference of £2,059,000. Its average rate of return was 4.30%, against 3.94% for the three-month SONIA, a benchmark based on short-term interest rates between banks. The paper says the difference was "primarily due to longer sustained levels of higher interest rates throughout the year and higher balances than forecast". It does not give an equivalent breakdown for South.

news_drafts.headline: South Oxfordshire: 67 of 131 open internal audit actions past deadline, including eight Priority 1
news_drafts.lead:
South Oxfordshire's Joint Audit and Governance Committee has been told that 67 of the 131 open actions from internal audit, the council's in-house check on whether its controls work, were past their deadlines on 25 September 2026. Eight of the 16 open Priority 1 actions, which the auditors define as fundamental to the integrity of a process, are overdue.

The report links the overdue Priority 1 actions to site visit audits at Abbey House, Cornerstone and Beacon. All three were rated Limited assurance. Together they produced 46 of the 87 actions in the 2025/26 audit plan, 19 of them Priority 1. Of the 131 open actions, 96 were raised in 2025/26 and 2026/27. Since the last update, internal audit raised 65 new actions and 105 were closed, while 51 are implemented and awaiting evidence or validation. Audits of cyber security, including artificial intelligence, and of travel and expenses were also rated Limited. The cyber audit raised nine actions, two of them Priority 1. The travel audit raised four, one of them Priority 1.

The papers report better news on other fronts. Neither South Oxfordshire nor Vale of White Horse had any external borrowing at 31 March 2026. South Oxfordshire's authorised limit, the most total debt it has told itself it will not exceed, was set at £35m. A licensing audit rated Substantial assurance, up from Satisfactory when it was last audited in May 2017. It found no discrepancies in fees tested against the 2025-26 schedule and raised only four Priority 3 actions.

Auditors also found some licence changes lacked evidence of compliance with statutory advertising requirements. None of the 39 licensing procedures reviewed had documented review dates, and some had not been reviewed since December 2020. In a separate audit, rated Substantial, five of 20 sampled report checklists (one South Oxfordshire, four Vale) lacked specialist officer sign-off on the implications sections.

news_drafts.headline: South Oxfordshire's budget surplus masks service-level overspend
news_drafts.lead: South Oxfordshire Council forecasts a £184,000 underspend for the year. But the council's own accounts show this surplus is entirely due to higher-than-expected investment income. Services across the council are forecast to overspend by £714,000. The council expects to receive £899,000 more in investment income than budgeted because interest rates have remained elevated. It holds £55m in investments. Without this extra investment income, the council would face a £714,000 overspend. The financial position is therefore dependent on the interest rate environment remaining high.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Vale Treasury activities 2025-26, 08/10/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Treasury team adopted ICD investment platform in February 2026, which early indications suggest increased money market fund income by 0.2%.
findings.detail: The treasury team pursued multiple proactive cash management tactics throughout 2025/26 to maximize returns within the constraints of a low-risk investment strategy. These included reviewing cash balances in late afternoons to invest same-day receipts via call accounts, intensive daily monitoring during the Christmas holiday period (deploying £33 million across both councils), and adoption in February of the ICD investment platform which allows daily selection from multiple money market funds. Early analysis indicates the platform transition contributed to a 0.2% increase in money market fund income.
findings.matters: Active optimization of returns on treasury reserves reflects capable financial management and demonstrates commitment to generating value from operating balances without accepting additional risk.
findings.figures: £33 million deployed during Christmas holiday period; ICD platform increased money market fund income by 0.2%
findings.quote: In February the councils moved to using 'ICD', an investment platform which allows the choice from a number of money market funds each day. Early indications suggest using this platform has led to an increase in money market income of 0.2 per cent.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Vale Treasury activities 2025-26, 08/10/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council maintained usable cash-backed reserves of £61.4 million at 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: The council's usable cash-backed reserves totaled £61.4 million at year-end 31 March 2026, including capital grants received in advance of spend. This reserve level is distinct from the average investment holdings of £188 million during the year, which represents working capital needed for operational cashflow timing. The £61.4 million in usable reserves provides capacity to meet obligations and absorb financial pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy is a key creditworthiness indicator; £61.4 million in usable reserves demonstrates the council's financial buffer and capacity to service obligations.
findings.figures: Usable cash-backed reserves £61.4 million (31 March 2026); average investment holdings £188 million during 2025/26
findings.quote: the council's usable cash backed reserves, which at 31 March 2026 totalled £61.4million including capital grants received in advance of spend

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Vale Treasury activities 2025-26, 08/10/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Council outperformed peer group in treasury investment returns while maintaining low-risk portfolio of local authority and money market fund investments.
findings.detail: The council is part of the MUFG benchmarking club and outperformed the peer group average by 0.40 basis points. The investment portfolio is predominantly conservative, with funds held with local authorities and money market funds. Fixed-term and call account deposits outperformed the SONIA benchmark by 0.36%, and the CCLA property fund outperformed its benchmark by 0.34%.
findings.matters: Outperforming peer benchmarks while maintaining conservative risk profile demonstrates financial competence and suggests treasury management is well-equipped to safeguard both operating balances and any borrowed funds.
findings.figures: Peer group outperformance 0.40 basis points; fixed-term deposits outperformance 0.36%; CCLA property fund outperformance 0.34%
findings.quote: The council outperformed the average of the group by 0.40 basis points with a very low risk profile of investments, mainly with local authorities and money market funds.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Vale Treasury activities 2025-26, 08/10/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Investment income outperformed budget by £2.1 million, driven by sustained higher interest rates and larger cash balances.
findings.detail: The council achieved actual treasury investment interest of £6,401k against a budget of £4,342k, an outperformance of £2,059k (£2.1 million). The average rate of return achieved was 4.30%, exceeding the 3-month SONIA benchmark of 3.94% by 36 basis points. This outperformance was primarily due to longer sustained levels of higher interest rates throughout the year and higher cash balances than had been forecast.
findings.matters: Additional investment income of £2.1 million provides unexpected financial resources available for services, reserves, or offsetting other budget pressures, improving the council's overall financial position.
findings.figures: Actual interest earned £6,401k vs budget £4,342k; outperformance £2,059k (£2.1 million); actual return 4.30% vs SONIA benchmark 3.94%, 36 basis points above benchmark
findings.quote: The actual rate of return achieved was £2.1 million higher than the original budget. This is primarily due to longer sustained levels of higher interest rates throughout the year and higher balances than forecast

findings.paper_title: Appendix E - Treasury Invest as at 31 March 2026, 08/10/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Vale of White Horse holds a £3 million investment in Gravesham Borough Council with an escalator rate, a structured product with uncertain future returns.
findings.detail: Vale of White Horse's portfolio includes a £3 million investment in Gravesham Borough Council dated 17/05/2027 with an escalator rate instead of a fixed rate. Escalator-rate instruments have returns that adjust according to a formula, creating valuation uncertainty. This is an uncommon instrument choice for council treasury holdings.
findings.matters: Escalator-rate products create future valuation uncertainty and are less common in council treasury operations, which typically favour fixed-rate investments for predictability.

daily_post.lead: Peer outperformance in treasury management with a lower-risk approach demonstrates above-average financial management capability relative to comparable councils.
